findings.title: Failed work is marked complete and can be committed
findings.body: The `finally` block completes the offset even when `result_processor` raises. The commit loop can then advance Kafka past a result whose processing failed, permanently losing it. This also contradicts the strategy's guarantee that offsets are committed only after successful processing; only mark the offset complete after successful handling, or preserve a failure state that prevents committing it.

findings.title: Legitimate Kafka offset gaps block commits indefinitely
findings.body: This tracker requires every integer offset between received records to appear in `all_offsets`. Kafka consumers can legitimately observe gaps—for example, when control records or compacted records are skipped. If records arrive at offsets 100 and 102, this loop stops at 101 and never commits 102 or later, even after all delivered records finish. Track the ordered offsets actually delivered rather than requiring numerically contiguous offsets.

findings.title: Unbounded queues provide no backpressure
findings.body: `queue.Queue()` defaults to unlimited capacity, so `submit()` never blocks when workers fall behind. The Kafka consumer can continue ingesting while queued results and offset-tracking state grow without bound, risking excessive memory use or an OOM. Use bounded queues and propagate backpressure to the consumer.

findings.title: Closing a strategy permanently shuts down the factory's shared queue pool
findings.body: The queue pool is owned by the factory and reused by strategies created through `create_with_partitions`, but closing any strategy shuts that shared pool down. After a partition reassignment or other strategy recreation, the factory can create a new strategy that submits to queues whose workers have exited, so results stop being processed. Keep the pool alive for the factory lifetime or recreate it when a new strategy is created.

findings.title: Shutdown neither reliably wakes workers nor drains queued items
findings.body: On Python versions before 3.13, `queue.Queue` has no `shutdown()` method; the caught `AttributeError` leaves workers blocked in `get()` and each pool shutdown leaks its daemon threads. On Python 3.13, setting `worker.shutdown` before shutting down the queues causes workers to exit after their current item rather than draining queued work. Use a shutdown mechanism supported by the project's Python versions and ensure pending work is handled before workers exit.
